name: Rosemary oil hair growth

lead: Rosemary oil is an aromatic oil from the rosemary plant that people massage into the scalp, usually diluted in a carrier oil or added to shampoo, with the aim of encouraging thicker hair and slowing thinning. It is a popular plant-based add-on for those wary of or supplementing drug treatments.

The best-known human data is a 2015 randomised trial in men with pattern hair loss in which hair counts after six months did not differ significantly between rosemary oil and 2% minoxidil lotion. Dermatologists quoted in coverage note that 2% is a weaker strength than the 5% commonly recommended, and that the trial had no placebo group.

paras: Users commonly dilute a few drops of the essential oil in a carrier oil, or use rosemary-containing products, and massage it into the scalp on a regular schedule over months. Scalp massage itself was part of the 2015 trial routine.

Essential oils contain compounds such as camphor and cineole that can irritate skin or cause allergic reactions in some people, and itching and dandruff increased in the rosemary group of the 2015 trial. Undiluted essential oil is generally not applied to skin.

angle.text: People apply diluted rosemary oil to the scalp, often alongside massage, hoping to slow thinning and gain density. In the 2015 trial, hair counts in the rosemary group rose modestly over six months.

lead: Rosemary oil for hair growth is the practice of applying rosemary (Salvia rosmarinus) essential oil, or products containing it, to the scalp in the hope of improving hair density. Rosemary oil is already used in perfumes, shampoos and aromatherapy products, and it contains roughly 10 to 20 percent camphor.[1]

The main human evidence is a 2015 randomised comparison published in Skinmed that assigned men with androgenetic alopecia to rosemary oil or 2% minoxidil lotion for six months. Its authors reported no significant difference between groups at three or six months.[2]
Interest rose sharply with social media coverage of rosemary oil, with dermatologists quoted in reviews treating it as a possible complement to established treatments rather than a replacement.[2]
infobox: Diluted in carrier oil, or in shampoos and serums

paras: Rosemary oil is applied to the scalp diluted in a carrier oil, or comes in shampoos and serums. In the 2015 trial participants massaged the preparation into the scalp twice daily.[2]
Proponents point to rosemary's long traditional use in hair care and to compounds such as carnosic acid, which a laboratory study found could inhibit 5-alpha reductase, the enzyme that makes DHT.[2]

A randomised trial by Panahi and colleagues (Skinmed, 2015) enrolled 100 men with androgenetic alopecia, split into two groups of 50, comparing rosemary oil with 2% minoxidil over six months. The paper reported no significant difference between groups at three or six months; the rosemary group averaged about 6 more hairs in the counted area (about 5.5%) and the minoxidil group about 2 (1.6%). Itching and dandruff were more common in the rosemary group, and itching also increased with minoxidil.[2]

A critical review of the paper by a cosmetic-science writer raised points including the absence of a placebo group, inconsistencies in reported numbers, seasonal effects over the trial period, and that the participants' twice-daily scalp massage was also a variable. Dermatologists quoted there, Leona Yip and Mark Strom, noted that 5% minoxidil is the more commonly recommended strength.[2]

A laboratory study (Murata et al., 2013) reported that a rosemary leaf extract and its compound 12-methoxycarnosic acid inhibited 5-alpha reductase in vitro; the same review notes that the extract needed far more material than finasteride for a similar effect.[2]

The review notes that essential oils can contain allergens and irritants, naming camphor, carnosol and cineole, and that irritation could itself aggravate hair shedding; it describes heavy dilution in a carrier oil as the usual practice.[2]

timeline.event: Period during which the Panahi trial was run (April 2010 to June 2011).[2]
